questions.prompt: In line 1, canō is best identified as

options.text: first person singular present active indicative
first person singular perfect active indicative
first person singular present passive indicative

questions.explanation: canō is the first person singular present active indicative of canō, canere. The long ō is the personal ending -ō; the perfect would be cecinī. Vergil announces his subject in the present: “I sing”, not “I sang”.

questions.prompt: In line 2 (Ītaliam … vēnit), Ītaliam is best understood as

options.text: accusative of place to which, without a preposition

questions.explanation: vēnit is intransitive and cannot take a direct object. Ītaliam is an accusative of place to which with the preposition omitted — a poetic construction Vergil uses constantly, and one AP tests often. Compare Lāvīnia … lītora in the same sentence.

questions.prompt: In line 4, superum is
questions.explanation: superum is the shortened (syncopated) genitive plural of superī, “the gods above” — so vī superum is “by the violence of the gods above”. Reading it as an accusative singular leaves vī without a genitive and produces nonsense. Syncopated genitive plurals in -um for -ōrum are common in epic.

questions.prompt: In line 4, memorem agrees with
questions.explanation: memorem is accusative singular, and the only accusative singular noun available is īram; saevae is genitive singular agreeing with Iūnōnis. The interlocked order (saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram) is deliberate: the adjectives are separated from their nouns and interwoven, a favourite Vergilian effect. Grammar, not proximity, decides agreement.

questions.prompt: In line 5, dum conderet urbem is best translated

options.text: until he could found a city
while he was founding a city

questions.explanation: dum with the subjunctive expresses anticipation or purpose — “until he might/could found”. dum with the indicative would mean simple contemporaneous time (“while”). The subjunctive conderet is the deciding evidence, and the sense fits: the founding is the goal all the suffering serves.

questions.prompt: The repetition of multum (line 3) and multa (line 5) at the head of successive clauses is an example of
questions.explanation: Anaphora is the repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses or phrases. Here it stacks up the sheer quantity of Aeneas’ suffering — first on land and sea, then in war — before the sentence finally reaches its purpose in dum conderet urbem. Chiasmus would be an ABBA arrangement; litotes is understatement by double negative; asyndeton is the omission of conjunctions.

questions.prompt: The Albānī patrēs of line 7 refer to

options.text: the kings of Alba Longa, from whom Rome’s founders descended
the Trojan elders who fled with Aeneas
the priests of the Alban Mount

questions.explanation: Alba Longa was the city founded by Ascanius, and its line of kings connects Aeneas to Romulus and so to Rome itself. The three-stage progression in lines 6–7 — genus Latīnum, Albānī patrēs, moenia Rōmae — compresses the whole legendary history from Aeneas’ landing to the city, which is exactly the claim the poem exists to make.

questions.prompt: In line 1 (Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs), the first foot is
questions.explanation: Ar-ma vi- scans long–short–short: the a of Arma is long by position (before rm), and both syllables of -ma vi- are short. That is a dactyl. Vergil opens the poem with a dactyl on arma, giving the first word metrical prominence as well as positional prominence.

questions.prompt: The question at 1.11 (tantaene animis caelestibus īrae?) most directly

options.text: raises the theological problem the poem will spend twelve books answering
accuses Juno of a crime against Jupiter
signals that the narrator does not believe in the gods
marks the end of the invocation and the start of the narrative

questions.explanation: The line asks whether such anger can really exist in divine minds. It is not an accusation but a genuine problem: the poem must reconcile a benevolent fate with a goddess who tortures a pious man. The question is left hanging until Jupiter and Juno settle terms in Book 12, which is why quae iam finis erit, coniunx? (12.793) reads as its answer.

questions.prompt: In the phrase dissimulāre etiam spērāstī, perfide, tantum / posse nefās (4.305–306), nefās is best translated
questions.explanation: nefās is what is contrary to divine law — the negative of fās. Dido is not calling Aeneas’ departure merely unlucky or dishonest; she is framing it as an offence against the gods, which is why she can appeal to them in the lines that follow. “Misfortune” would be cāsus; “lie” would be mendācium.

questions.prompt: In 4.314 (per ego hās lacrimās dextramque tuam tē), the arrangement of per … tē is an example of

options.text: tmesis and hyperbaton, separating the preposition from its object for emotional effect
anastrophe, placing the preposition after its object

questions.explanation: per governs tē, but Vergil throws ego and a long string of appeals between them, so the oath formula is stretched almost to breaking. The dislocation enacts Dido’s agitation — she cannot get to the end of her own sentence. Anastrophe would put per after tē; there is no ellipsis of the verb, since ōrō follows.

questions.prompt: The best literal translation of neque ego hanc abscondere furtō / spērāvī (ne finge) fugam (4.337–338) is

options.text: nor did I hope to conceal this flight by stealth — do not imagine it
nor do I hope that this flight can be hidden by theft — do not pretend
nor did I hope to be hidden from this flight by a thief — do not lie
nor did I expect this stolen flight to be concealed — do not deceive yourself

questions.explanation: spērāvī is perfect, so “did I hope”, not “do I hope”. furtō is an ablative of means, “by stealth”, not “theft” as an agent. hanc … fugam is the object of abscondere across the intervening words. ne finge is a poetic negative command, “do not imagine (it)”.

questions.prompt: Which Latin best supports the claim that Aeneas presents his departure as compelled rather than chosen?
questions.explanation: nōn sponte means “not of my own accord”, and it is the closing word of the whole speech — the position gives it weight. The other options are true statements about the speech but do not bear on compulsion: they concern its brevity or his memory of Dido. On the exam, choosing evidence that actually supports the specific claim is what row-scoring rewards.

questions.prompt: In 4.331–332 (ille Iovis monitīs immōta tenēbat / lūmina), the placement of immōta … lūmina around the line break chiefly

options.text: enacts the fixity it describes by suspending the phrase across the enjambment
creates a caesura in the fifth foot

questions.explanation: immōta is held back from its noun until the next line, so the reader’s eye is itself held — the word order performs the immobility of Aeneas’ gaze. This is a standard way Vergil makes syntax do descriptive work. A golden line has a fixed adjective–adjective–verb–noun–noun pattern, which this is not.

questions.prompt: In 6.851–853, regere, impōnere, parcere and dēbellāre are all
questions.explanation: mementō (“remember”) takes a complementary infinitive, and all four infinitives hang from it. Recognising this is what holds the sentence together: they are not four separate commands but four objects of one imperative. There is no accusative subject, so indirect statement is ruled out; historical infinitives take a nominative subject and narrate.

questions.prompt: In 6.853, subiectīs is
questions.explanation: parcō takes the dative, so subiectīs is dative plural — “to spare the conquered”. The contrast with superbōs, which is accusative as the object of dēbellāre, is the point of the line: two verbs, two different constructions, deliberately balanced.

questions.prompt: The relationship of parcere subiectīs to dēbellāre superbōs (6.853) is best described as
questions.explanation: Two opposed ideas — mercy and destruction — are set out in matching verb + object form, so the structure is parallel and the sense antithetical. Chiasmus would require the order to reverse (ABBA); it does not. The balance is what makes the line quotable and what makes the poem’s ending, where Aeneas does not spare a suppliant, so pointed.

questions.prompt: In conceding that others will excel at sculpture, oratory and astronomy (6.847–850), Anchises is contrasting Rome with
questions.explanation: The three arts named — bronze and marble sculpture, forensic oratory, and mapping the heavens — are precisely those in which Greek achievement was acknowledged as supreme. Anchises concedes cultural pre-eminence to Greece in order to claim a different and, he argues, higher art for Rome: government. The move is a commonplace of Augustan self-definition.

questions.prompt: In 6.16.4 (mater mea indicat eī appārēre nūbem), appārēre nūbem is

options.text: a result clause with the infinitive

questions.explanation: indicō introduces indirect statement: nūbem is the accusative subject and appārēre the infinitive, “that a cloud was appearing”. Reading nūbem as the direct object of indicat leaves appārēre stranded. Recognising the accusative + infinitive is one of the highest-frequency skills the exam tests in Pliny.

questions.prompt: In 6.16.5, the comparison of the cloud to a pīnus depends on the tree’s

options.text: tall bare trunk spreading into branches at the top

questions.explanation: Pliny spells the comparison out in §6: longissimō velut truncō ēlāta in altum quibusdam rāmīs diffundēbātur — raised on a very long trunk and then spreading into branches. He means the Mediterranean umbrella pine, whose shape is exactly that of an eruption column. It is the reason this type of eruption is called “Plinian”.

questions.prompt: In 6.16.5, ūsus ille sōle is best rendered

options.text: he, having been used by the sun
the use of the sun by him
he being useful in the sun

questions.explanation: ūtor is deponent: the perfect participle ūsus is active in meaning, “having used / having taken”, and it governs the ablative sōle. Translating it passively is the classic deponent error. The idiom ūtī sōle means to take a sunbath — part of the bathing routine Pliny describes.

questions.prompt: Which Latin best supports the claim that Pliny presents his uncle’s decision as a deliberate move from scholarship to rescue?

options.text: vertit ille cōnsilium et quod studiōsō animō incohāverat obit maximō
nūbem inūsitātā et magnitūdine et speciē

questions.explanation: The sentence explicitly contrasts what he began with a scholar’s mind (studiōsō animō incohāverat) with what he carried through with the greatest spirit (obit maximō) — the turn is stated, not implied. The other options are true details but do not name the change of purpose; vertit cōnsilium is the pivot of the whole letter.

questions.prompt: Pliny the Elder was at Misenum because

options.text: he commanded the Roman fleet stationed there
he owned an estate on the slopes of Vesuvius
he had been sent by Titus to investigate the earthquakes

questions.explanation: Misenum, at the northern end of the Bay of Naples, was the base of the western imperial fleet, and Pliny the Elder was its prefect — classem imperiō praesēns regēbat (6.16.4). That command is what puts warships at his disposal and turns a scientific curiosity into a rescue operation.

questions.prompt: Pliny’s account of reading Livy during the earthquake (6.20.5) functions chiefly to

options.text: present his own composure as a deliberate contrast to the panic around him
explain how he later wrote the letter
show that he did not understand the danger
criticise his mother for her anxiety

questions.explanation: The detail is placed immediately beside the friend from Spain rebuking both of them, so the calm is staged against alarm; Pliny even reports the rebuke and says he went on reading. Whether the poise is real or literary, its function in the letter is self-presentation. He is seventeen, and the anecdote is doing the same work as his uncle’s bath and dinner in 6.16.

questions.prompt: In 6.20.9 (mare in sē resorbērī vidēbāmur), the form vidēbāmur means
questions.explanation: videor in the passive regularly means “seem”, not “be seen”, and takes an infinitive. So the sense is “we seemed to see the sea being sucked back”. Translating it as a true passive produces the wrong subject and loses the careful hedging Pliny uses throughout for things he could not verify.

questions.prompt: In 6.20.14 (audīrēs ululātūs fēminārum, īnfantum quirītātūs, clāmōrēs virōrum), the arrangement is best described as

options.text: a tricolon, with variation in the order of noun and genitive

questions.explanation: Three parallel members make a tricolon; Pliny varies it by switching the order within the second and third members rather than repeating a fixed pattern, which keeps the list from sounding mechanical. There is no repeated opening word, so it is not anaphora. The effect is to fill the darkness with distinct, sourceless sounds.

questions.prompt: In 7.27.5, sonus ferrī means “a sound of iron”. The form ferrī here is
questions.explanation: ferrī is ambiguous in form — it is both the genitive of ferrum and the present passive infinitive of ferō — and Pliny’s sentence is a favourite AP trap. Here sonus needs a genitive to complete it, and the ghost is dragging chains, so “of iron” is right. Always let the syntax of the sentence decide between homographs.

questions.prompt: In 7.27.5, sī attenderēs ācrius uses the imperfect subjunctive to express

options.text: a generalising “if you listened”, with an indefinite second person
a contrary-to-fact condition in present time

questions.explanation: The second person singular subjunctive with an indefinite “you” is a standard way of describing what anyone would experience — “if you listened closely”. It is not contrary to fact: people did listen, and did hear it. Reading it as unreal makes the ghost story report something that never happened, which is the opposite of Pliny’s point.

questions.prompt: In 7.27.5, the imperfects reddēbātur and appārēbat are best understood as

options.text: a single completed action in the past
actions going on when the ghost arrived

questions.explanation: The whole point of the haunting is that it recurred night after night until the house was abandoned. The iterative imperfect carries that, and English needs “would appear” or “used to appear” to render it. A simple past (“appeared”) reduces a standing haunting to one incident and loses the reason the house stood empty.

questions.prompt: Which detail most directly explains why the haunting stops?

options.text: the bones are collected and buried at public expense with proper rites
Athenodorus proves he is not afraid
the magistrates dig up the courtyard
the philosopher marks the spot with grass and leaves

questions.explanation: Roman belief held that the unburied dead could not rest. The story turns on that: the ghost leads Athenodorus to its own remains, and once the bones receive rīte conditīs mānibus — burial with due rites — the house is quiet. Digging and marking are steps toward the remedy; the remedy itself is the burial.

questions.prompt: Pliny frames the whole letter as a question to Sura about whether ghosts

options.text: have a real existence and form of their own, or take shape only from our fear
are punished by the gods for their crimes

questions.explanation: The opening asks whether phantoms exist and have their own shape and some divine power, or whether they are inānia et vāna and take form ex metū nostrō. Framing an entertaining story as a philosophical enquiry is a standard epistolary move: it dignifies the material and gives the letter a reason to exist beyond the anecdote.

questions.prompt: Trajan’s replies in Book 10 differ from Pliny’s letters chiefly in being

options.text: markedly shorter and plainer, focused on a decision

questions.explanation: The contrast is one of the most testable features of Book 10. Pliny builds context, justifies himself and defers at length; Trajan answers in a few sentences and decides. Compare 10.5–10.6 with 10.7, or 10.33 with 10.34: the emperor’s brevity is itself an assertion of authority.

questions.prompt: In 10.37, ut aquam habeant expresses
questions.explanation: ut with the subjunctive after a statement about spending money again gives the goal of the expenditure — “so that they may have water”. Result would require an anticipatory word such as tam, ita or sīc in the main clause, and there is none. Distinguishing purpose from result by looking for those signposts is a standard AP task.

questions.prompt: Trajan refuses the firefighters’ guild at Nicomedia (10.34) primarily because

options.text: associations of any kind tend to become political clubs
the cost would fall on the imperial treasury
he doubts that fires are a serious danger there
Pliny had exceeded his authority in proposing it

questions.explanation: Trajan says it directly: whatever name is given them and for whatever reason, such groups will shortly become hetaeriae — political clubs — and that province has already been troubled by factions. It is not a financial or a technical objection but a political one, and it is the clearest surviving statement of imperial suspicion of collegia.

questions.prompt: In the passage, quibus rēbus cognitīs is

options.text: a dative of reference with a participle

questions.explanation: A noun and a participle together in the ablative, grammatically independent of the main clause, form an ablative absolute: “these things having been learned” or, better English, “when this became known”. The connecting relative quibus simply links back to the previous sentence and does not make it a relative clause.

stimulus.latin: Quibus rēbus cognitīs, Caesar apud mīlitēs contiōnātus est et eōs cohortātus est ut prīstinam virtūtem retinērent.
stimulus.citation: Adapted prose, in the style of the sight-reading section

questions.prompt: The best literal translation of eōs cohortātus est ut prīstinam virtūtem retinērent is

options.text: he urged them to keep their former courage
he was urged by them to keep their former courage
he urged that they had kept their former courage
having urged them, he kept his former courage

questions.explanation: cohortātus est is deponent, so it is active in meaning with Caesar as subject and eōs as object. ut + imperfect subjunctive after a verb of urging is an indirect command: “to keep”. Option two mistakes the deponent for a true passive; option four turns the finite verb into a participle.

stimulus.latin: Quibus rēbus cognitīs, Caesar apud mīlitēs contiōnātus est et eōs cohortātus est ut prīstinam virtūtem retinērent.
stimulus.citation: Adapted prose, in the style of the sight-reading section

questions.prompt: In Catullus 85 (Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris), the opening two words are an example of
questions.explanation: Two opposed verbs are set immediately side by side with nothing between them, so the contradiction is the whole point — the poem is built on it. Anaphora needs a repeated opening word; hyperbaton needs separated words that belong together; synchysis is interlocked ABAB word order.

stimulus.latin:
Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.

questions.prompt: In Catullus 85, excrucior is

options.text: first person singular present passive indicative
first person singular present active indicative
third person singular present passive indicative

questions.explanation: The ending -or marks the first person singular present passive: “I am tortured”. The passive is the point of the poem — the speaker is not doing something but having something done to him, which is why the poem ends on it. A third person singular passive would be excruciātur.

stimulus.latin:
Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.

questions.prompt: The juxtaposition of nesciō with sentiō in Catullus 85 chiefly conveys that the speaker

options.text: feels the contradiction without being able to explain it
is deceiving the person he addresses
blames the gods for his condition

questions.explanation: nesciō denies knowledge and sentiō asserts perception, and the two sit in the same line: he cannot account for what is happening but he can feel it happening to him. That gap between understanding and experience is the poem’s subject, and excrucior completes it by making him the object of the process.

stimulus.latin:
Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.

questions.prompt: According to Roman tradition, the monarchy fell and the Republic began after

options.text: the rape of Lucretia and the resulting revolt led by Lucius Junius Brutus
a plebeian secession over unpaid debts
the defeat of Carthage in the Third Punic War

questions.explanation: Roman tradition dates the fall of the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, to 509 BCE, sparked by the rape of Lucretia and the revolt she inspired. Caesar's assassination (44 BCE) ends the Republic, not begins it; the plebeian secessions belong to the later Struggle of the Orders; the Punic Wars are unrelated to the monarchy's fall.

questions.prompt: The Twelve Tables (c. 451–450 BCE) mattered to plebeians chiefly because they

options.text: published the law publicly, ending patrician monopoly on knowing it
granted plebeians the right to hold the consulship

questions.explanation: Before the Twelve Tables, legal knowledge and procedure were an unwritten patrician preserve. Publishing the law was a major plebeian gain in the Struggle of the Orders, even though full political equality (like consular eligibility) came only later, through further reforms.

questions.prompt: A Roman senator's public career (the cursus honorum) moved through magistracies in which order?
questions.explanation: The cursus honorum ran from the more junior quaestorship (financial administration) through the praetorship (judicial and military command) to the consulship, the summit of the ordinary career — with a minimum age and required interval at each step.

questions.prompt: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps and the catastrophic Roman defeat at Cannae belong to
questions.explanation: The Second Punic War is the one remembered for Hannibal's invasion of Italy from the north and the disaster at Cannae (216 BCE); Rome nonetheless won by carrying the war to Africa, where Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE.

questions.prompt: Cato the Elder's refrain "Carthago delenda est" ("Carthage must be destroyed") is grammatically an example of

options.text: the passive periphrastic of obligation (gerundive + sum)

questions.explanation: dēlenda est is a gerundive (dēlenda, agreeing with the feminine Carthāgō) plus a form of sum — the passive periphrastic construction expressing necessity, "must be destroyed". No agent is expressed because Cato's point needed none.

questions.prompt: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, reforming tribunes of the 130s–120s BCE, are chiefly remembered for

options.text: proposing land redistribution to the poor, and being killed for it
writing Rome's first published law code

questions.explanation: Both Gracchi brothers, as tribunes, pushed land reform for Rome's landless poor and were killed by their political opponents — the first political killings in Rome in centuries, and a precedent of violence that shaped the following century of Roman politics.

questions.prompt: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon (49 BCE) was significant chiefly because

options.text: a general was legally required to disband his army before entering Italy, and Caesar did not
it marked the final defeat of Carthage
it was the site of the Twelve Tables' drafting

questions.explanation: Roman law forbade a general from bringing an army into Italy proper under arms. By crossing the Rubicon with his legions, Caesar committed an irreversible act of war against the Roman state itself — hence his reported remark, alea iacta est, "the die is cast".

questions.prompt: Octavian's victory over Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium (31 BCE) led directly to

options.text: Octavian becoming sole ruler of the Roman world, later named Augustus
the restoration of the old Republic with no change in power

questions.explanation: Actium eliminated Octavian's last serious rival. By 27 BCE he had engineered the "restoration" of the Republic while retaining real power as princeps, taking the name Augustus — the beginning of the Principate under which Vergil wrote the Aeneid.

questions.prompt: The Roman title princeps ("first citizen"), which Augustus used instead of rex ("king"), was chosen because

options.text: rex carried poisonous associations with the monarchy the Republic had overthrown
princeps was a formal constitutional office with defined powers
the Senate required all rulers to use a Greek title
Julius Caesar had used the same title before him

questions.explanation: Rome's traditional hatred of kingship (dating to the legendary expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus) made rex politically toxic. princeps, "first citizen," was a title rather than a defined office — allowing Augustus to hold real, permanent power without appearing to claim a crown.

questions.prompt: The emperor reigning at the time of the eruption of Vesuvius (79 CE), Pliny's subject in his letters to Tacitus, was
questions.explanation: Titus (79–81 CE), son of Vespasian and second of the Flavian emperors, had only just succeeded his father when Vesuvius erupted. Trajan was the emperor decades later, to whom Pliny's Book 10 letters (from his Bithynian governorship) are addressed.

questions.prompt: A Roman household's Lares and Penates were

options.text: household gods, tended daily at a family shrine (the lararium)
the two annually elected chief magistrates
professional legal scholars who wrote opinions on the law

questions.explanation: The Lares and Penates were household/ancestral guardian spirits, worshipped daily at a small family shrine. Roman religion combined this intensely domestic, private layer with the large public state cult of gods like Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva.

questions.prompt: Roman manumission (the formal freeing of a slave) differed from freedom in many other slave societies chiefly in that

options.text: it created a full Roman citizen, whose own children were born entirely free
it was extremely rare and required an act of the Senate
freed slaves were expelled from Roman territory
it applied only to slaves born in Italy

questions.explanation: A manumitted Roman slave (a libertus) became a citizen, not merely a free non-citizen, and any children born to him afterward were born fully free with no lingering restriction — a path to integration many other slave-owning societies did not offer.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly shows a 2nd-declension neuter noun's nominative and accusative plural?
questions.explanation: Every neuter noun, in every declension, has identical nominative and accusative forms in both singular and plural. For 2nd-declension bellum, that plural form is bella — never bellōs, which would be a masculine accusative plural ending.

questions.prompt: The genitive singular of a 3rd-declension noun is important chiefly because it

options.text: reveals the noun's true stem, which the nominative singular often hides or alters
is always identical in spelling to the nominative plural
determines whether the noun is masculine or feminine
is the only case ending shared with the 1st declension

questions.explanation: 3rd-declension nominatives are wildly unpredictable (rēx/rēgis, corpus/corporis, homō/hominis) because of stem changes like rhotacism, a hidden nasal, or syncope. The genitive singular is where the real stem — the one every other case is built on — actually shows up.

questions.prompt: In fertur (as in the idiom "he is said"), fertur is best identified as

options.text: 3rd person singular present passive of the irregular verb ferō
3rd person singular present active of ferō
an impersonal verb with no personal ending

questions.explanation: ferō, ferre is highly irregular but still fully conjugated; fertur is its ordinary present passive 3rd singular, idiomatically "it is said/carried" — one of the most common idiomatic passive uses a student will meet.

questions.prompt: In a sentence like hortātur eōs ut fortiter pugnent ("he urges them to fight bravely"), the construction ut + subjunctive is

options.text: indirect command, after a head verb of urging

questions.explanation: hortor is a head verb of command/persuasion, and its content is expressed as ut + subjunctive — indirect command — not as an infinitive the way English "urges them TO fight" might suggest. iubeō is the one common exception that does take an infinitive instead.

questions.prompt: timeō nē hostēs veniant means

options.text: "I fear that the enemy will come" (I am afraid they WILL come)
"I fear that the enemy will not come"
"I feared that the enemy had come"
"I doubt that the enemy will come"

questions.explanation: After a verb of fearing, nē is affirmative in sense — the reverse of its usual negative force — so timeō nē veniant means "I fear THAT he will come", not "that he won't". ut after a fear verb would give the negative sense instead.

questions.prompt: A relative clause of characteristic (e.g. nēmō est quī hoc nesciat) is distinguished from an ordinary relative clause by

options.text: a subjunctive verb, marking the clause as describing a general type rather than one specific fact

questions.explanation: The subjunctive (nesciat, not nescit) signals that the clause characterizes a kind or type ("the sort of person who...") rather than stating a specific fact about one particular antecedent, which would use the indicative instead.

questions.prompt: In Carthāgō dēlenda est, the dative of agent (if one were added, e.g. nōbīs) would express

options.text: who must perform the necessary action
the means by which the action happens

questions.explanation: The passive periphrastic (gerundive + sum) regularly takes a dative of agent naming who is obligated to act: Carthāgō nōbīs dēlenda est, "Carthage must be destroyed BY US" — rendered more naturally in English as "we must destroy Carthage".

questions.prompt: sequitur, a 3rd-singular present form of the deponent verb sequor, should be translated

options.text: actively: "he follows" — deponent verbs are passive in form but active in meaning

questions.explanation: The single most important fact about a deponent verb is that every form, however passive it looks, is active in meaning. sequitur looks like an ordinary passive ("is followed") but actually means "follows" — sequor has no separate active voice at all.

questions.prompt: In section 13 (in remedium formīdinis dictitābat), the uncle says the fires were abandoned farmhouses burning. His purpose in saying so is

options.text: to blame the farmers for the eruption
to explain the eruption scientifically for his book
to persuade Pomponianus to sail at once

questions.explanation: in remedium formīdinis, “as a cure for fear”: the phrase gives the purpose. The admiral explains the flames away so that the household will not panic, the same calm he shows by bathing, dining and sleeping.

questions.prompt: In section 14, ut sī longior in cubiculō mora, exitus negārētur is best described as
questions.explanation: ita … oppleta surrēxerat, ut … negārētur: the courtyard had filled so high with ash and pumice that, had he stayed longer, the way out would have been blocked. ita signals result.

questions.prompt: In section 15, intrā tēcta subsistant an in apertō vagentur is best translated

options.text: they stay under the roofs and wander in the open
although they stood under the roofs, they wandered outside
so that they might stay indoors rather than wander
whether they should stay under cover or wander in the open

questions.explanation: After In commūne cōnsultant, the subjunctives subsistant and vagentur form a double indirect deliberative question: whether to stay … or (an) to wander. The council weighs collapsing houses against falling stones.

questions.prompt: In section 17, nigrior is

options.text: a comparative adjective, with omnibus noctibus as ablative of comparison

questions.explanation: nox omnibus noctibus nigrior dēnsiorque: “a night blacker and thicker than all nights”. The -ior ending marks the comparative; the ablative noctibus expresses “than”.

questions.prompt: In sections 21–22, Pliny stops before telling his own story because

options.text: he was not present at Misenum
Tacitus asked only about his uncle’s death, and a letter differs from history
he had already told it in an earlier letter

questions.explanation: nec tū aliud quam dē exitū eius scīre voluistī, and aliud est enim epistulam aliud historiam: he keeps to what Tacitus requested, leaving the choice of material to the historian. The story he holds back becomes Letter 6.20.

questions.prompt: In section 1, Pliny quotes quamquam animus meminisse horret, … incipiam, words of

options.text: Aeneas, beginning his story of the fall of Troy
Livy, at the start of his history

questions.explanation: The line is Aeneid 2.12–13, Aeneas about to tell Dido of Troy’s last night. Pliny casts his own escape from Misenum as an epic survivor’s tale, with a smile at the grandeur.

questions.prompt: In section 4, sī quiēsceret excitātūrus expresses

options.text: an indirect question about his mother
what Pliny intended: to wake her if she was sleeping

questions.explanation: The future participle excitātūrus gives intention: he was getting up “to wake her, if she was asleep”. They had each come to wake the other.

questions.prompt: In section 7, quodque in pavōre simile prūdentiae, aliēnum cōnsilium suō praefert, Pliny observes that frightened people

options.text: think following someone else’s plan is wisdom

questions.explanation: The crowd prefers another’s plan to its own, “which in panic looks like prudence”. It is a sharp, general remark about crowds, typical of Pliny’s moralizing asides.

questions.prompt: In section 9, the cloud is described as rupta in longās flammārum figūrās … fulguribus illae et similēs et maiōrēs erant. The comparison to lightning

options.text: shows that it was only a thunderstorm
is ironic, since there was no fire
makes the unfamiliar eruption imaginable through something familiar

questions.explanation: Pliny has no word for what he saw, so he reaches for lightning: “like it, and bigger”. Comparison to the familiar is how he makes the scene vivid for Tacitus’s readers.

questions.prompt: In section 12, posse enim iuvenem … bene moritūram is best described as

options.text: indirect statement reporting his mother’s words

questions.explanation: The accusatives iuvenem and sē with the infinitives posse and moritūram (esse) report what she said: a young man could escape; she, heavy with years, would die content.

questions.prompt: In section 14, alii parentēs aliī līberōs aliī coniugēs vōcibus requīrēbant is an example of
questions.explanation: aliī … aliī … aliī: the repeated word at the head of each phrase, three times, makes the crowd of voices in the dark audible, parents, children and spouses calling for one another.

questions.prompt: In section 14, the subjunctive precārentur in erant quī metū mortis mortem precārentur is used because

options.text: it is a relative clause of characteristic: “there were those who …”

questions.explanation: erant quī + subjunctive describes a kind of person: “there were people of the sort who prayed for death out of fear of death”. Note also the polyptoton mortis mortem.

questions.prompt: In section 17, Pliny says he could boast of not crying out, except that he believed

options.text: he and the whole world were dying together, a wretched but great comfort

questions.explanation: mē cum omnibus, omnia mēcum perīre (note the chiasmus) … magnō tamen mortālitātis sōlāciō: his courage, he admits, came from thinking everyone was dying with him.

questions.prompt: In section 9, similis vocantī: vocantī is

options.text: a present participle used as a noun, dative with similis

questions.explanation: vocāns, vocantis, the present participle, here in the dative after similis: the ghost beckoned “like someone calling”.

questions.prompt: In section 10, dēsertus herbās et folia concerpta signum locō pōnit is best translated

options.text: deserted, the grass and leaves were placed in the spot
the deserted place was marked by grass
he put a sign among the grass and leaves
left alone, he plucked grass and leaves and put them on the spot as a marker

questions.explanation: dēsertus agrees with the philosopher; herbās et folia concerpta is the object, “grass and leaves, plucked”; signum is in apposition, “as a sign”; locō is ablative of place without a preposition.

questions.prompt: Section 11 says the house was free of the ghost once the bones were buried rīte. This reflects the Roman belief that

options.text: ghosts haunt the houses of the guilty
chains keep the dead from wandering

questions.explanation: Proper burial rites (rīte conditīs mānibus) let the dead rest. Once the chained bones were buried at public expense, the haunting ended.

questions.prompt: In section 14, Pliny connects the haircuts in his household with

options.text: a dream sent by the gods
his escape from a charge Domitian would have pursued

questions.explanation: Defendants let their hair grow; cut hair, he infers, signaled that the danger hanging over him had passed. A libellus against him was found in Domitian’s desk after the emperor’s death.

questions.prompt: In section 1, quae mē nōn sunt passae … prōsequī: quae refers to
questions.explanation: quae picks up occupātiōnibus meīs: his business, which did not “allow” (passae sunt, from patior) him to go with her. The relative is feminine plural to match.

questions.prompt: In section 2, corpusculō is best understood as

options.text: an affectionate diminutive: “your poor little body”

questions.explanation: The diminutive -culum softens the word: Pliny worries tenderly over her frail health. It is one of the marks of affection in his letters to his wife.

questions.prompt: In section 4, Vereor omnia, imāginor omnia contains
questions.explanation: omnia ends both clauses (epistrophe), and there is no conjunction between them (asyndeton). The repetition makes his fear seem boundless.

questions.prompt: The last sentence, Erō enim sēcūrior dum legō, statimque timēbō cum lēgerō, suggests that

options.text: her letters will end his worry for good
he would rather not hear from her
her letters calm him only while he reads them
he will stop writing to her

questions.explanation: The future and future perfect set the two moments side by side: while reading, easier; once finished, afraid again. Hence his request for one letter a day, or even two.

questions.prompt: In section 1, quod prō mē libellōs meōs teneās: the subjunctive teneās is used because

options.text: the clause reports what Calpurnia wrote (indirect statement)

questions.explanation: The quod clause belongs to what Calpurnia says (Scrībis …): subordinate clauses inside reported speech take the subjunctive.

questions.prompt: In section 2, lēctitō means
questions.explanation: lēctitō is the frequentative of legō: repeated action. Pliny takes up her letters identidem … quasi novās, “again and again as if new”.

questions.prompt: In section 3, cuius litterae tantum habent suāvitātis, huius sermōnibus quantum dulcēdinis inest! is an example of

options.text: an argument from the lesser to the greater

questions.explanation: If her letters are so charming, how much sweeter her conversation must be: from the lesser (letters) to the greater (her presence). The exclamation ends on what he is missing.

questions.prompt: In section 3, licet hoc ita mē dēlectet ut torqueat: licet with the subjunctive means
questions.explanation: licet + subjunctive is concessive, “although”. ita … ut torqueat is a result clause: it delights him so that it torments him. Write anyway, he says.

questions.prompt: In 10.5, section 2, rogō dēs eī cīvitātem Rōmānam: dēs is subjunctive because

options.text: it is an indirect command with ut omitted
it is a jussive in its own sentence

questions.explanation: After verbs of asking, ut is often left out: rogō (ut) dēs, “I ask you to give”. Pliny uses the same form again in 10.6, rogō … tribuās.

questions.prompt: Pliny asks for citizenship for Harpocras because

options.text: he was a soldier in Pliny’s province
he cared for Pliny during a dangerous illness

questions.explanation: gravissimā valētūdine usque ad perīculum vītae vexātus iātralīptēn assūmpsī: the masseur-doctor nursed him through it, and Pliny can repay him only through the emperor’s favor.

questions.prompt: In 10.6, Pliny’s mistake was that

options.text: he asked for the wrong man
an Egyptian needed Alexandrian citizenship before Roman
he forgot to send the man’s age

questions.explanation: admonitus sum … dēbuisse mē ante eī Alexandrīnam cīvitātem impetrāre, deinde Rōmānam, quoniam esset Aegyptius. He had thought all foreigners were alike in this.

questions.prompt: In 10.6, section 1, quoniam esset Aegyptius: esset is subjunctive because

options.text: the reason is part of what the experts told him (reported reasoning)

questions.explanation: quoniam normally takes the indicative; the subjunctive marks the reason as part of what Pliny was told by those more experienced, not his own assertion.

questions.prompt: In 10.7, Trajan grants the request because

options.text: Pliny has already obtained Roman citizenship for the man
Harpocras is an Alexandrian by birth

questions.explanation: Sed cum … iam cīvitātem Rōmānam impetrāveris, huic quoque petītiōnī tuae negāre nōn sustineō: having given the greater gift, he will not refuse the lesser, though he grants it sparingly.

questions.prompt: In 10.37, section 1, novō impendiō est opus: impendiō is ablative because

options.text: opus est takes the ablative of the thing needed

questions.explanation: opus est + ablative: “there is need of new expense”. The Nicomedians, having wasted so much, need still more to have water.

questions.prompt: In 10.37, section 2, the water should come arcuātō opere so that

options.text: it can reach the higher parts of the city, not only the low ground

questions.explanation: nē tantum ad plāna cīvitātis et humilia perveniat: a negative purpose clause. Water must arrive high to serve the whole city.

questions.prompt: In 10.37, section 3, Pliny’s closing praise, ūtilitātem operis et pulchritūdinem saeculō tuō esse dignissimam, appeals to

options.text: Trajan’s interest in a reign remembered for useful and beautiful public works

questions.explanation: Governors framed requests in terms of the emperor’s glory. An aqueduct both useful and beautiful is “most worthy of your age”.

questions.prompt: In 10.90, section 1, Sinōpēnsēs … aquā dēficiuntur: aquā is ablative because

options.text: dēficior is used with an ablative of the thing lacking (separation)

questions.explanation: In the passive, dēficior means “to be short of”, with the ablative of what is lacking: the people of Sinope are short of water.

questions.prompt: In 10.90, section 2, valdē sitientis colōniae is an example of
questions.explanation: A colony cannot be thirsty; its people can. Giving the town a human need makes Pliny’s practical request vivid.
